section.title: David King Over All Israel
section.sectionRationale: The long wait ends: all the tribes gather at Hebron and anoint David king over all Israel, fulfilling the LORD's word that he would shepherd His people. David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem and makes it his capital, grows greater because the LORD is with him, and twice inquires of the LORD before defeating the Philistines. The movement is the summit of David's rise, the throne finally given by God to His shepherd-king.
section.thesis: After years of waiting, God gives David the throne over all Israel, establishes him in Jerusalem, and grants him victory, so that David grows greater not by his own strength but because the LORD of Hosts is with him and has exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: all Israel anoints David king at Hebron, verses 1 to 5; the capture of Jerusalem and David's growing greatness, verses 6 to 12; David's expanding household, verses 13 to 16; and two victories over the Philistines won by inquiring of the LORD, verses 17 to 25.

verses.text: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood.

Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And to you the LORD said, ‘You will {{raah|shepherd}} My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.’”
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a {{berit|covenant}} before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

units.label: David captures Jerusalem
units.note: the LORD of Hosts was with him

verses.text: Now the king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who inhabited the land. The Jebusites said to David: “You will never get in here. Even the blind and lame can repel you.” For they thought, “David cannot get in here.”
Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David).

On that day he said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must use the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are despised by David.” That is why it is said, “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace.”
So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all the way around, from the supporting terraces inward.
And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him.
Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David.
And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.

units.label: David's household grows
units.note: more sons and daughters in Jerusalem

verses.text: After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.

units.label: Two victories over the Philistines
units.note: the LORD has gone out before you

verses.text: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went down to the stronghold.
Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go up,” replied the LORD, “for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand.”
So David went to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me.” So he called that place Baal-perazim.
There the Philistines abandoned their idols, and David and his men carried them away.
Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD, who answered, “Do not march straight up, but circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees.
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because this will mean that the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”
So David did as the LORD had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.

raah.gloss: To shepherd, to tend, feed, and lead a flock; used of a king caring for his people. The LORD's word is that David will shepherd Israel, drawing on David's literal work as a shepherd to define kingship as guardianship, not exploitation. The image runs forward to the LORD as Shepherd, Psalm 23, and to Christ, the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a solemn binding agreement sealed before God. David makes a berit with the elders of all Israel before the LORD, so that his kingship rests on a mutual, God-witnessed bond rather than mere conquest. The word reaches its height in the everlasting covenant God makes with David in chapter 7 and is fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.

basic.context: This chapter is the summit of David's long rise. After seven and a half years reigning over Judah alone, and years of patient waiting since Samuel first anointed him, all the tribes of Israel now come to Hebron. They call David their own flesh and blood, recall that he had always led Israel in battle, and quote the LORD's word that David would shepherd His people. The elders make a covenant with him before the LORD and anoint him king over all Israel. David then captures the Jebusite fortress of Jerusalem, a city belonging to no tribe, and makes it his capital, the City of David. He grows greater and greater, the text says, because the LORD of Hosts is with him, and he comes to realize that God has established his kingdom for the sake of His people. When the Philistines attack to crush the new king, David does not presume; he inquires of the LORD before each battle and wins both by obeying God's specific directions. The chapter raises the questions of how David finally comes to the throne, why Jerusalem matters, and what the source of David's greatness really is.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative celebrating the establishment of David's kingdom, told to show that it was God's doing. It is not a promise that every faithful person will rise to prominence, nor does David's taking of more wives and concubines, verse 13, receive approval; the narrator reports it, and it will bear bitter fruit later, running against the law's warning that a king should not multiply wives. What the chapter presents for imitation is David's habit of inquiring of the LORD before acting and his recognition that his greatness came from God for the sake of God's people, not for his own glory.
basic.originalLanguages: The tribes ground their appeal in the LORD's word that David will raah, shepherd, His people, a word that defines the king as a shepherd who guards and feeds the flock rather than a lord who exploits it. David seals his kingship by making a berit, a covenant, with the elders before the LORD, so that his reign rests on a God-witnessed bond. Both words, shepherd and covenant, look forward to the Davidic covenant of chapter 7 and to Christ, the Good Shepherd of the new covenant.
basic.typology: David, born in Bethlehem and long anointed but only now enthroned over all Israel in Jerusalem, the shepherd-king whom the LORD makes great for the sake of His people, is a clear type of Christ. Jerusalem becomes the city of the great King, and David's throne there becomes the seat of a kingdom that Scripture will trace to the Messiah who reigns from the true Zion.
basic.christ: David is the shepherd-king given the throne by God, established in Jerusalem, growing great not by his own power but because the LORD is with him. This foreshadows Jesus, the Son of David and true Shepherd of His people, who is enthroned as King not for His own sake but for the sake of the people God gives Him. As David asked the LORD before every battle and won by God going out before him, so Christ did only the Father's will and won His victory as the Father worked through Him.
basic.god: God is the one who gives David the throne, fulfilling His long-standing word, and who is present with David so that he grows greater and greater. God establishes the kingdom not for David's glory but for the sake of His people Israel, showing that He raises up rulers to serve His purposes and care for His flock. And God is the warrior who goes out before David against the Philistines, so that the victories are His gift, not merely David's skill.
basic.crossReferences: First Samuel 16 records the anointing now fully realized. Psalm 78 celebrates God taking David from the sheepfolds to shepherd His people. Deuteronomy 17 warns kings not to multiply wives, a warning David's growing household begins to strain. And the New Testament presents Jesus as the Son of David and Good Shepherd who reigns for His people, in Matthew 2 and John 10.
basic.oneStory: The shepherd God chose long ago is finally king over all Israel, enthroned in Jerusalem, made great because the LORD is with him. This high point of the story, a covenant king reigning for the good of God's people from the city of the great King, points forward to Jesus, the Son of David and Good Shepherd, whose everlasting kingdom is established for the sake of all God's people.

context.literary:
The chapter is arranged as a sequence of foundation stories, throne, capital, household, army, each answering the same rhetorical shape, an achievement followed by the narrator's own explanation of its true cause. It also deliberately answers chapter 3's earlier list of sons born in Hebron with a second list, verses 13 to 16, of sons born in Jerusalem, so that the reader tracks David's rising household alongside his rising kingdom at each successive capital, one list marking a king still contested, the other marking a king finally secure, or so the placement of the list implies.

Verse 17 ties enthronement directly to threat, the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and they all went in search of him, making external opposition an immediate narrative consequence of the internal event just celebrated, as though the text wants readers to notice that being made king by God's people does not exempt a king from having to be delivered by God's power in the same breath.

The two Philistine battles are also told with a deliberate asymmetry that rewards attention. The first divine answer is brief and general, go up, I will surely deliver them, verse 19, while the second is unusually specific and strange, wait until you hear marching in the treetops, verse 24, a shift from a plain yes to an image nobody could have anticipated on their own, teaching by its very form that obedience to God cannot be reduced to a formula that worked once and can simply be repeated.
context.historical:
Jerusalem's Jebusite defenders had held the city since long before David, an unconquered holdout stretching back to the days after Joshua; Judges 1:21 records that the tribe of Benjamin, in whose territory the city technically lay, had failed to dislodge the Jebusites there, so that by David's day the fortress had resisted roughly four centuries of intermittent Israelite pressure, making its capture here a genuinely striking military and symbolic achievement rather than a mopping up operation.

Hiram's gift of cedar, carpenters, and masons, verse 11, reflects Tyre's long-standing role as a major Mediterranean source of cedar timber and skilled building craft, a partnership that will matter far more directly a generation later when Hiram supplies the materials for Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 5. Its earliest appearance here, building a king's house rather than a temple, shows the relationship between Israel's throne and Phoenician trade beginning well before the more famous temple project.

The Valley of Rephaim southwest of Jerusalem carried its own old association: Rephaim were remembered elsewhere in Scripture as a people of unusual size or strength from before Israel's conquest, Genesis 14:5, Deuteronomy 2:11 and 20, so the very ground where David twice defeats the Philistines bore a name recalling ancient giants, fitting territory for the man who had once brought down Goliath in his youth.
context.canonical:
The phrase David coins here, the City of David, verse 7 and 9, becomes the standing formula the books of Kings use for centuries afterward to mark where each descendant of David is buried, beginning with David himself, 1 Kings 2:10, so that a name given at the moment of conquest becomes the fixed address of the whole dynasty's memory. Psalm 132 later reflects on the events of this chapter and the ark's coming to Jerusalem in chapter 6, recalling David's oath to find a dwelling for the LORD and celebrating God's own choice of Zion, this is My resting place forever, Psalm 132:13 and 14, turning David's military and political achievement here into the basis of a whole strand of temple centered worship and hope.

The prophets inherit and intensify this Zion theology. Isaiah can picture Jerusalem as the city from which the LORD's instruction will go out to all nations, Isaiah 2:2 and 3, precisely because this chapter first made it David's, and therefore Israel's, capital rather than a Jebusite holdout with no covenant history. Every later biblical hope centered on Jerusalem traces back structurally to the specific, unglamorous military campaign narrated in these few verses, culminating in Revelation's picture of a heavenly city coming down from God, Revelation 21:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is answering a question a later Israelite reader would almost certainly have been asking: what made David's kingdom, and by extension the whole Davidic line the reader's own history depended on, legitimate in the first place? The answer given here is deliberately layered, tribal consent, verses 1 and 2, formal covenant, verse 3, military conquest, verses 6 to 9, international recognition, verse 11, and repeated divine confirmation through inquiry and victory, verses 19 to 25, so that no single strand alone has to carry the weight of the claim.

Removing any one of these, tribal support without divine word, or military success without covenant, would leave a kingdom looking exactly like every other ancient Near Eastern power grab; the writer wants all of them held together, because together they describe a throne established the way Israel believed a throne should be established, by the convergence of the people's recognition and God's own initiative, not by either one substituting for the other.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
David's practice of inquiring before every battle, verses 19 and 23, is often lifted straight into a devotional principle, always ask God before acting, and there is real substance to that reading, but the text's own detail resists turning it into a rigid technique: the two answers David receives are not the same, and the second victory depends on watching for a sign, marching in the treetops, that has no parallel anywhere else in Scripture and was never meant to become a repeatable formula for future battles.

What is prescriptive is the posture, not the method, a king who assumes he needs fresh instruction rather than applying yesterday's plan to today's problem. Likewise the international alliance with Hiram, verse 11, describes a strategic and probably wise diplomatic move without commanding readers to seek out comparable alliances; the chapter simply is not offering a manual for statecraft, only a record of how, this time, God's people and God's blessing converged.

debates.question: How should we read David's taking of more wives and concubines in verse 13?

views.label: A reported compromise, not an endorsement
views.case: The narrator simply records David's expanding harem without praise, and Deuteronomy 17:17 had warned that a king must not take many wives lest his heart go astray; the very next chapters show David's household becoming a source of rivalry, lust, and violence, so the detail is best read as an early crack in an otherwise glorious chapter, honestly reported rather than approved.

views.label: A conventional mark of royal status in its setting
views.case: In the ancient Near East a large royal household signaled power and secured alliances, so some read verse 13 chiefly as a historical note on David's rising stature; even so, Scripture's larger judgment, and the bitter fruit in David's family, exposes it as description of a practice that God's law had cautioned against.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage is descriptive, not prescriptive; the glory of the chapter belongs to God's establishing of David, while the note about wives quietly foreshadows the troubles that David's own household will bring, reminding readers to weigh even a great king's actions against God's word.

debates.question: What does the Jebusites' taunt about the blind and the lame in verse 8 mean, and how should the saying that followed it be read?

views.label: A boast about the fortress, later abbreviated into a proverb
views.case: The Jebusites mean that their walls are so strong that even disabled defenders, hardly a serious garrison, could repel any attack, a taunt about David's chances rather than a statement about disability itself; the saying it produced, the blind and the lame will never enter the palace, functioned afterward as a proverb for stubborn resistance, detached from any comment on disabled people generally, and the BSB footnote allows the whole line to be rendered simply those who are enemies of David.

views.label: A troubling saying that needs careful handling regardless of its origin
views.case: Whatever the taunt originally meant, its wording has at times been read as though Scripture itself treats blindness and lameness as disqualifying, a reading the rest of the Bible will not support, since the same book later shows David bringing the lame Mephibosheth to eat continually at the king's table, 2 Samuel 9:13, and the prophets picture the lame gathered in and made into a strong remnant rather than excluded, Micah 4:6 and 7.

debates.bearing: The verse describes a battlefield insult and its resulting saying, not a divine verdict on disability; reading it alongside David's later kindness to Mephibosheth keeps the taunt in its place as an enemy's boast rather than letting it become a theological claim Scripture nowhere else supports.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 10's report that David became greater and greater repeats a doubled Hebrew construction found also in Genesis 26:13, where Isaac, in almost identical wording, became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy. Hebrew intensifies ongoing growth this way, pairing a verb of going with a verb of increase, and its use in only a handful of similar passages marks the growth described as an unfolding process under God's blessing rather than a single achievement credited to the man himself; both verses go on to name the LORD, not human striving, as the reason for the increase.

The Jebusite fortress falls, according to verse 8, by way of what the BSB calls the water shaft, a rare Hebrew word that appears elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only once, in Psalm 42:7, deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls. Whatever the exact structure David's men climbed through, the word's near total absence elsewhere means translators reconstruct its specifics mostly from context; what is certain is that a city confident in its visible defenses fell through a hidden channel nobody thought to guard, an old pattern in Scripture where confidence in obvious strength gives way before an overlooked way in.

Verse 9's supporting terraces render the Millo, a technical architectural term for a filled, terraced structure built up a hill's slope to support buildings above it. The same term appears at Shechem generations earlier, Beth-millo, the house of the Millo, Judges 9:6, and again in Jerusalem itself when Solomon later builds his own Millo as part of his great construction projects, 1 Kings 9:15 and 24, so that David is not merely occupying a captured city but beginning an engineering project later kings, Solomon most of all, will keep building on, literally and politically.

And the name David gives his first battlefield, Baal-perazim, the LORD bursts out, verse 20, uses a verb of breaking through, the same root behind the name Perez, Judah's son and an ancestor of David, whose birth in Genesis 38:29 is marked with the midwife's cry, you have broken out first, and behind Micah's later vision of one who breaks open the way going up before God's gathered people, Micah 2:13, an image many Christian interpreters have read as messianic. A single verb of breaking through ties David's battlefield to his own ancestor's birth and to a prophet's picture of the King who leads His people out through every barrier ahead of them.

typology.type: The shepherd exalted to a throne he did not build
typology.fulfillment: David comes from tending sheep to being told, you will shepherd my people Israel, verse 2, language that reframes kingship as a task done for the flock rather than a status held over it. Jesus takes up the identical image, I am the good shepherd, John 10:11, and roots His right to shepherd God's people in laying down His life for them rather than in any conquest, so that the type sharpens exactly where it might have stayed merely political, into a shepherd who dies for, rather than merely rules, His flock.

typology.type: A city belonging to no tribe becomes the seat of the kingdom
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem is captured from the Jebusites, not inherited from any of the twelve tribes, and becomes neutral ground where a unified people can gather under one king, verses 6 to 9. That pattern, a capital that belongs to no single faction so that it can belong to everyone, anticipates the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God, Hebrews 12:22, gathered from every tribe and nation rather than granted by inheritance to any one of them, a city Revelation describes coming down prepared as a bride for a King greater than David, Revelation 21:2.

typology.type: Victory won by inquiry, not by David's own tactical genius
typology.fulfillment: Twice David asks the LORD exactly how to fight, and twice the LORD's specific instructions, including the strange sign of marching sounds in the balsam trees, verse 24, are what actually secure the victory. This dependence anticipates Christ, who said the Son can do nothing by Himself but only what He sees the Father doing, John 5:19, so that even the pattern of obedience that wins David's battles becomes a rehearsal for the deeper obedience by which Christ wins His.

typology.type: The Philistines' idols abandoned on the field
typology.fulfillment: David's men carry off the gods the Philistines left behind at Baal-perazim, verse 21, a small detail showing false gods unable even to protect themselves, let alone their worshippers. It anticipates the disarming of every power opposed to Christ, stripped and put to open shame at the cross, Colossians 2:15, and looks forward to the day every idol will finally be discarded before the true King alone remains standing.

study.christ:
Everything in this chapter that makes David great, the tribes' recognition, the capital, the victories, is credited by the narrator to one cause repeated twice in seven verses: the LORD God of Hosts was with him, verse 10, and the LORD had established him, verse 12. That refusal to let David's own competence carry the weight of the story is exactly the pattern the Gospels use for a greater son of David, whose miracles are done, He insists, not by His own authority alone but because the Father who dwells in Him is doing His work, John 14:10, and whose kingdom the tribes of Israel, and eventually every tribe and nation, will likewise recognize only because God has already declared it, not because Jesus campaigned for the throne.

The shepherd language of verse 2 is the most direct thread to Christ in the whole chapter. Israel's elders quote back to David words the LORD had spoken, you will shepherd my people Israel, defining kingship from the start as care for a flock rather than command over subjects, and Jesus takes up that exact title for Himself, the good shepherd who knows His sheep and lays down His life for them, John 10:11 and 14, going further than David ever could, since David's shepherding, whatever its virtues, never required him to die for the flock he led.

Jerusalem's capture matters too. A city that belonged to no tribe becomes David's, and then all Israel's, capital, a piece of neutral ground that a divided people can gather around without any tribe claiming superiority over another. Something similar and far larger happens in Christ, in whom Jew and Gentile, insiders and outsiders to Israel's ancient inheritance, are built together into one household of God, Ephesians 2:19 to 22, a spiritual Jerusalem belonging, in the end, to no single people's claim of ownership but to everyone who is His.
study.god:
This chapter names God's presence as the explicit, stated cause of David's success twice in close succession, verses 10 and 12, a repetition that functions almost like a corrective note attached to a story that could easily be read the wrong way. Every other detail in the chapter, the elders' negotiation, the daring capture of a supposedly impregnable fortress, the building project, the Philistine victories, could be told as a tale of one man's competence; the narrator interrupts twice to insist otherwise, that competence is real but causation belongs to the LORD of Hosts.

God is also, in this chapter, a God who answers specific questions with specific instructions rather than only general promises. Should I go up, will you deliver them, verse 19, gets the direct answer, go up, I will surely deliver them; the second battle gets an entirely different, oddly precise instruction, wait for a sound in the treetops before you move, verse 24. The two battles are not won the same way, which matters, because it shows a God who is present in the details of obedience, not merely in a broad providence that leaves David to improvise the tactics himself.

At the same time, this chapter's honesty keeps God's blessing from becoming an endorsement of everything David does within it. Verse 13 records, without a word of praise, that David took more wives and concubines once he settled in Jerusalem, directly against the warning already given for Israel's future king, that he must not take many wives for himself, Deuteronomy 17:17. The same God who is establishing David's throne for the sake of His people is not thereby approving every choice David makes as he grows into it; blessing and obedience are shown here as related but not identical, a distinction the rest of David's story, and especially the Bathsheba narrative not far ahead, will make painfully clear.

Finally, God's stated purpose in exalting David, for the sake of His people Israel, verse 12, reframes the whole chapter's celebration. The throne is not given because David deserves glory for its own sake; it is given because God intends good for a people, which is precisely the logic that will govern every king worth following after him, and the logic Jesus states plainly when He says He came not to be served but to serve, Mark 10:45.

crossReferences.note: Isaac became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy, the same doubled construction used of David's rise, a grammatical pattern Scripture reserves for describing increase that belongs to God's blessing rather than to human striving alone.

The rare word rendered water shaft in David's capture of Jerusalem appears only one other time in the Hebrew Bible, here of roaring waterfalls, deep calling to deep, so obscure a term that its exact meaning in either passage is reconstructed mostly from context.

The Millo at Shechem, called here Beth-millo, the house of the Millo, was a fortified precinct built the same way as the terraced structure David raises in Jerusalem, showing this was a recognized method of ancient civic building rather than an invention unique to David's city.

Solomon later builds his own supporting terraces, the Millo, in Jerusalem as part of his great building projects, continuing literally the engineering David began after capturing the city, so that father and son are shown extending the same physical structure across two reigns.

The midwife's cry at the birth of Perez, Judah's son and an ancestor of David, you have broken out first, uses the same root behind Baal-perazim, tying the name David gives his battlefield victory back to the very family line the LORD had chosen.

Micah pictures one who breaks open the way going up before God's gathered people to lead them out through the gate, an image built on the same root as David's Baal-perazim and long read by Christian interpreters as a portrait of the Messiah leading His people through every barrier.

The law's specific warning that Israel's king must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray, is exactly what verse 13 quietly records David beginning to do in Jerusalem, a detail the narrator neither praises nor excuses.

Jesus claims the shepherd title spoken over David in verse 2, but deepens it past anything David's story ever required of him, the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, a shepherding that costs the Shepherd everything.

Paul describes Jew and Gentile built together into one household of God, a far greater unifying of once divided peoples than even Jerusalem's neutral ground achieved when it became the single capital of all Israel's tribes.

Jesus states the very logic verse 12 already applies to David, that a throne exists for the good of the people rather than the glory of the one who holds it, even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.

study.oneStory:
This chapter is the hinge the whole David story has been leaning toward since Samuel poured oil on a shepherd boy's head in an obscure village years before. Every delay since then, the years fleeing Saul, the seven and a half years reigning over Judah alone, the war with Ish-bosheth's house, the murders of Abner and Ish-bosheth that David refused to profit from, was leading here, to all Israel gathering at Hebron to call the shepherd what God had already called him. The long wait was never wasted time; it was the shape the promise took on its way to being kept.

From here the story's center of gravity shifts decisively to Jerusalem, a city that belonged to no tribe and now belongs, in a sense, to all of them, the place where the ark will soon rest, chapter 6, where the covenant will be given its fullest form, chapter 7, and where, centuries later, the true Son of David will be crucified and rise, turning David's captured hill into the ground from which the whole world's redemption is finally accomplished.

But the chapter also plants, almost in passing, the seed of the story's next great trouble. Verse 13's quiet note about more wives and concubines sits right beside the celebration of God's blessing, a reminder that even a king this favored, this shepherd this thoroughly established by God, is not thereby safe from his own appetite, and the chapters just ahead, Bathsheba, Absalom, will show exactly what that appetite costs. The Bible tells its long story of redemption unflinchingly, refusing to let even its high points hide the cracks already forming, because the hope of the story was never David's own perfect obedience but the greater Shepherd David's throne was always waiting for.

quiz.q: On what basis do all the tribes come to make David king?

options.text: They are his own flesh and blood, he had always led Israel in battle, and the LORD had said David would shepherd His people.
options.note: Verses 1-2 gather all three grounds, climaxing in the LORD's word that David would shepherd Israel.

options.text: David had conquered Jerusalem and proven himself the strongest available leader.
options.note: Jerusalem is taken after the coronation, and the tribes appeal to kinship and the LORD's word, not to conquest.

options.text: The LORD had promised that David would shepherd and rule His people.
options.note: True and central, but this option omits the kinship and David's proven leadership that the tribes also cite.

options.text: Samuel returned and commanded the tribes to crown David.
options.note: Samuel had died earlier; the tribes come of their own accord, appealing to the LORD's earlier word, not a fresh command from Samuel.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say David grew greater and greater?

options.text: Because the LORD God of Hosts was with him, establishing his kingdom for the sake of His people.
options.note: Verses 10 and 12 credit David's greatness to the LORD's presence and purpose for His people.

options.text: Because David was a brilliant military strategist who never lost a battle.
options.note: David's skill is real, but the text attributes his greatness to the LORD being with him, not to strategy alone.

options.text: Because God was with him and had exalted his kingdom.
options.note: True, but this option omits the striking purpose clause, that God exalted the kingdom for the sake of His people, not David's glory.

options.text: Because Hiram of Tyre made him wealthy with cedar and craftsmen.
options.note: Hiram's gifts are a sign of David's rising standing, not the cause of his greatness, which the text credits to the LORD.

quiz.q: What does David do before each battle with the Philistines?

options.text: He inquires of the LORD, and he wins by obeying God's specific directions, even circling behind them at the balsam trees.
options.note: Verses 19-24 show David inquiring and obeying, so the LORD goes out before him.

options.text: He relies on his experience and attacks the Philistines the same way both times.
options.note: David asks the LORD each time, and God gives different instructions for the second battle, which David obeys.

options.text: He asks the LORD whether and how to fight before engaging the enemy.
options.note: True, but this option omits the striking detail that David wins because the LORD Himself goes out before him to strike the enemy.

options.text: He consults his commanders and then trusts the LORD for the outcome.
options.note: The text stresses David inquiring of the LORD directly, not consulting his commanders, before each battle.

quiz.q: Why is David's choice of Jerusalem as his capital significant?

options.text: The Jebusite fortress belonged to no tribe, making it a unifying capital, and David made it the City of David, the seat of the kingdom.
options.note: Verses 6-9 show David taking neutral Jerusalem and establishing it as his royal city.

options.text: Jerusalem was already the religious center of Israel with the temple standing there.
options.note: There was no temple yet; David brings the ark later, and Solomon builds the temple, so the city's religious role is only beginning.

options.text: David captured a strong, central stronghold and made it his royal city.
options.note: True, but this option omits that its tribe-neutral location helped unite Israel and that it became the enduring City of David.

options.text: It was David's birthplace, which made it the natural royal city.
options.note: David was born in Bethlehem, not Jerusalem; he chose Jerusalem for its strategic and unifying value.

quiz.q: How does David as shepherd-king in Jerusalem point to Christ?

options.text: He foreshadows Jesus, the Son of David and Good Shepherd, enthroned as King for the sake of God's people and reigning from the true Zion.
options.note: David's shepherd-kingship in Jerusalem anticipates Christ, John 10:11 and Hebrews 12:22.

options.text: He shows that God's kings must always expand their kingdoms by conquest.
options.note: The chapter credits God, not conquest, and Christ's kingdom advances by His shepherding love, not mere expansion.

options.text: He pictures a king who reigns for the good of God's people rather than his own glory.
options.note: True, but this option omits the specific shepherd and Zion imagery that so clearly points to Christ the Good Shepherd.

options.text: He proves that greatness comes to those who seize their opportunities boldly.
options.note: The chapter teaches the opposite; David's greatness is God's gift because the LORD was with him, not the fruit of seizing opportunity.

questions: The tribes finally acknowledged what God had said about David years earlier. Where are you waiting for others to recognize something God has already spoken over your life, and how do you wait well?

David realized that God had established him not for his own sake but for the sake of His people. How does it reframe your position, gifts, or influence to see them as given for others rather than for yourself?
Before each battle David inquired of the LORD rather than trusting his experience. Where are you relying on your own track record instead of seeking God freshly?
The chapter credits David's greatness to the LORD being with him. When you succeed, how quickly do you name God as the source, and how might you cultivate that habit?

Even in this glorious chapter, David's growing household plants a seed of future trouble. Where might a choice that seems to signal blessing actually be a compromise you need to weigh against God's word?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote allows the phrase about the 'lame and blind' to be rendered those 'who are enemies of David'; the saying reflects the Jebusite taunt and became a proverb, and should not be read as contempt for the disabled as such.
The BSB footnote explains that Baal-perazim means 'the Lord Bursts Out,' commemorating David's words that the LORD had burst through his enemies like a flood.
The BSB footnote notes that the starting point of the pursuit reads 'Gibeon' following the Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 14:16, while the Hebrew reads 'Geba,' two nearby places.
